prompt: Which field of `@Component` decides the tag you write in a template to use the component?

choices.text: `templateUrl`, which names the file the tag comes from
choices.why: That names the component's own template, not the tag other templates write.

choices.text: `selector`
choices.why: Right. `app-week-summary` is written as `<app-week-summary />`.

choices.text: The class name, lower-cased and hyphenated
choices.why: The CLI derives both from what you typed, but Angular reads the selector.

choices.text: `imports`, whose first entry is the component itself
choices.why: `imports` lists what the template uses, never the component itself.

prompt: `week-summary.css` says `p { font-weight: 600; }`. Which paragraphs on the page become bold?

choices.text:
Every `

` on the page, because CSS is global
choices.why: Angular rewrote the rule to `p[_ngcontent-…]`, so it is not global.

choices.text: Only those inside `WeekSummary`'s own template, nowhere else
choices.why: Right. They carry the `_ngcontent-` attribute the rewritten rule asks for.

choices.text: Those in `WeekSummary` and in every component it contains
choices.why: A child component's elements carry the child's own attribute, not the parent's.

choices.text: None, until the rule is also written in `styles.css`
choices.why: The rule applied; `look --styles` showed it in the page's stylesheets.

prompt: Angular's rewriting of a component's styles so that they apply to its own template only is called view ___.
A component in a codebase written in 2023 says `standalone: true`. One written in 2026 says nothing about it. What is the difference between them?

choices.text: None: standalone became the default in Angular 19
choices.why: Right. The line was needed before 19 and is redundant after.

choices.text: The 2026 one belongs to a module, since it does not say standalone
choices.why: That was true before 19. Today a module-based component says `standalone: false`.

choices.text: The 2023 one cannot be used by a 2026 application
choices.why: Standalone components from 2023 work in today's applications.

choices.text: The 2026 one has no template
choices.why: Standalone and templates are unrelated.

prompt: `npx ng build` failed with `NG8001: 'app-week-summary' is not a known element`, in `week.html`. Where does the fix go?

choices.text: In `WeekSummary`, which should export itself
choices.why: A standalone component has nothing to export; the one using it imports it.

choices.text: In `app.ts`, because `App` is the root
choices.why: `App`'s imports serve `App`'s template, and the tag is in `Week`'s.

choices.text: In `week.ts`, in the `imports` list of the `Week` decorator
choices.why: Right. The component that owns the template imports what it uses.

choices.text: In `angular.json`, which lists the project's components
choices.why: `angular.json` does not list components.

prompt: A component's class calls a function from `dates.ts` in a method, and its template never mentions it. Where must the function be imported?

choices.text: In the decorator's `imports`, so Angular can find it
choices.why: The decorator's list is for the template, and the template does not use the function.

choices.text: Only in an `import` line at the top of the file
choices.why: Right. Code in the class is TypeScript, and TypeScript's own `import` is enough.

choices.text: In both, as with a component
choices.why: A component is used by the template, which is why it needs both. A function used only in code does not.

choices.text: In `app.config.ts`, as a provider
choices.why: Providers are for things to be injected; lesson 10 is about them.

prompt: Match what a template uses with how it appears in the template.
In a module-based application, what decides which components a template may use?

choices.text: The component's own `imports`
choices.why: In that model a component has no list of its own.

choices.text: The module that declares the component
choices.why: Right. Its declarations and the exports of its imports are the scope.

choices.text: `angular.json`, which lists the modules
choices.why: `angular.json` names files and builders.

choices.text: Whichever module bootstraps the application
choices.why: Each component's scope is its own declaring module's, not the root's.

prompt: Match each field of `@NgModule` with what it lists.

pairs.right: the pieces that belong to this module
modules whose exported pieces its templates may use
what other modules may use from this one

prompt: A colleague's `SharedModule` declares forty buttons and pipes and exports them all, and thirty feature modules import it. What does the lesson say this costs?

choices.text: Each import makes a copy of the forty pieces in the bundle
choices.why: The bundle carries each piece once; the cost is not in bytes.

choices.text: The build fails past a fixed number of exports
choices.why: There is no such limit.

choices.text: Nothing; it is the recommended pattern today
choices.why: The lesson presents it as the cost standalone was introduced to remove.

choices.text: No component shows what it really depends on
choices.why: Right. Every component may use all forty, so none of them says which it uses.

prompt: Put the three modes of the standalone migration in the order the lesson runs them.
After `convert-to-standalone`, `SessionList` moved from `declarations` to `imports` in `AppModule`. What does that show?

choices.text: Modules import standalone components too
choices.why: Right. That is one of the two bridges that let a migration go one file at a time.

choices.text: The migration made a mistake that the next step undoes
choices.why: The application built and ran with that arrangement.

choices.text: `SessionList` became a module
choices.why: It is still a component; standalone components can sit in a module's `imports`.

choices.text: `declarations` only accepts the root component
choices.why: It accepts any component that belongs to the module.

prompt: Why was `App` not converted by the first step?

choices.text: Its template is too large to migrate
choices.why: Template size plays no part in the migration.

choices.text: The migration only converts generated components
choices.why: It converted `SessionList`, and would convert hand-written ones too.

choices.text: It is the component the module bootstraps, and that is step 3's work
choices.why: Right. `standalone-bootstrap` converted it and deleted `AppModule`.

choices.text: `App` was already standalone
choices.why: It said `standalone: false` until step 3.

prompt: After the three steps, `main.ts` provides `importProvidersFrom(BrowserModule, AppRoutingModule)`. What would you do with it?

choices.text: Leave it: the migration is the reference for how code should look
choices.why: The lesson says a migration keeps the app running and the tidying is yours.

choices.text: Delete the line, because standalone apps need no providers
choices.why: The router still has to be provided somehow.

choices.text: Replace it with `provideRouter(routes)`, and drop `BrowserModule`
choices.why: Right. That is the shape the planner's `app.config.ts` already has.

choices.text: Move it into every component's `imports`
choices.why: Component imports are for templates; providers go to the application.

prompt: A library you need ships only an NgModule, `ChartsModule`, which exports a `<chart>` component. How does a standalone component use `<chart>`?

choices.text: It cannot, until the library ships a standalone version
choices.why: Modules work in a standalone component's `imports`.

choices.text: It puts `ChartsModule` in its own `imports`
choices.why: Right. The template may then use everything the module exports.

choices.text: It wraps the module in `importProvidersFrom` in `app.config.ts`
choices.why: That takes a module's providers, not the components it exports.

choices.text: It declares `ChartsModule` with `standalone: false`
choices.why: `standalone` is a property of components, not a way of using modules.

prompt: Match what a module-based application imports with what a standalone application provides instead.

pairs.left: a library module with no such function

prompt: In a codebase half-way through its migration, a template fails with `NG8001` for `<app-badge>`. The component that owns the template says `standalone: false`. Where do you look first?

choices.text: In that component's `imports`
choices.why: A component with `standalone: false` has no template scope of its own.

choices.text: In `app.config.ts`, for a missing provider
choices.why: An unknown element is a template-scope problem, not a provider one.

choices.text: In `angular.json`, whose list of components may be out of date
choices.why: There is no such list.

choices.text: In the module that declares it, and whether that module imports something exporting `app-badge`
choices.why: Right. In the old model, the module is the scope.

prompt: `look --a11y body` listed two headings and a paragraph. What did it list for the components themselves?

choices.text: One group per component, named by its selector
choices.why: The tree had no entry for any component.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right. A component's tag carries no role, so a screen reader hears only what is inside.

choices.text: A region for `App` only, because it is the root
choices.why: `App` drew a heading, and the tree shows only that.

choices.text: A warning that custom elements are not accessible
choices.why: No warning; custom elements are simply transparent.

prompt: How many tests did `ng test` run, in total, at the end of this lesson?
A test creates `App` with `TestBed.createComponent(App)`. Which components does it build?

choices.text: Only `App`, with empty placeholders for the others
choices.why: Unless you replace them on purpose, the real components are built.

choices.text: `App` and `Week`, but not `WeekSummary`, which is two levels down
choices.why: Depth does not matter; each template builds what it uses.

choices.text: All three: `App`, `Week` and `WeekSummary`, each one real
choices.why: Right. `App`'s template uses `Week`, whose template uses `WeekSummary`.

choices.text: Every component in the project, generated or not
choices.why: Only those reached through the templates.

prompt: You generate `CourseCard` and write `<app-course-card />` in `week.html`. Before you build, what else is needed?

choices.text: Add `CourseCard` to `App`'s imports, since `App` is the root
choices.why: The tag is in `Week`'s template, so `Week` imports it.

choices.text: `CourseCard` added to the `imports` of `Week`
choices.why: Right. And the TypeScript `import` line at the top of `week.ts`.

choices.text: Declare `CourseCard` in an NgModule
choices.why: The planner has no modules; standalone components need none.

choices.text: Nothing; the CLI adds it to every template that uses it
choices.why: The CLI only updates a module in module-based projects.
